title: Arlette et Jean Gabin  (Arlette and Jean Gabin)

segments.t: On her way out after being dismissed, Camille notices a dog playing with a contract. His owner is Arlette, one of the agency's senior agents, and their first conversation begins awkwardly. Hear the scene in French first; the short questions will help you follow it.
Je passais par là. Il jouait avec un contrat.
J'en doute. Jean Gabin déteste les contrats.
Il n'a jamais joué avec un contrat.
Moi, c'est Camille. Je pars aujourd'hui.
On dit que vous êtes la plus grande imprésario de Paris.
Let's walk through it. Camille rushes in and tries to rescue the paper from the dog's teeth.
'No! Let go of the contract!' Camille gives a short instruction without a separate 'you'. She uses the familiar form when speaking to the dog.
'What are you doing?' The opening question expression asks 'what'. Arlette uses the familiar 'you' in her direct question to Camille.
'Look, here's your owner.' Camille says this to the dog, not to Arlette, so again it's the casual 'you'. The word she uses for 'owner' is the feminine one, literally the dog's 'mistress'.
'I was walking by.' Literally 'I was passing through there'. The ending of the action word tells you it was going on in the background, an ongoing past action.
'He was playing with a contract.' Same background past tense, same ending sound. Arlette is not convinced.
J'en doute. Jean Gabin déteste les contrats.
'I doubt it. Jean Gabin hates contracts.' The short piece attached to 'I' stands for the claim Camille has just made. French keeps that reference before 'doubt'.
Il n'a jamais joué avec un contrat.
'He has never played with a contract.' Here the negative pattern changes: instead of plain 'not', the second little word means 'never'. Then Arlette gets suspicious.
'Did Andréa send you?' Literally 'is it Andréa who sends you?'. Arlette thinks Camille might be spying for another agent.
'No, not at all.' Camille gives a quick, firm denial. And now Camille realises who she's talking to.

'Are you Arlette Azémar?' Here's the contrast to listen for. Camille uses the polite 'you' with Arlette, an older woman and a famous agent. So in this scene, one says casual 'you', and the other answers with the polite one.
'Yes. And you?' And this time it's the casual 'you' again, the stressed form you use on its own.
'I'm Camille.' Literally 'me, it's Camille'. It's the easiest, most natural way to introduce yourself.
'I'm leaving today.' The present form of 'leave' can describe a departure happening now or soon. The final word locates it on this day.
On dit que vous êtes la plus grande imprésario de Paris.

'People say you're the greatest impresario in Paris.' 'The greatest' is built with 'the most big'. The first little word means 'people' or 'one', a very common way to say 'they say'. Arlette waves it off.
'No need to flatter me!' This shortened expression leaves out a subject and a form of 'have'. The action 'flatter' follows a linking word, with 'me' placed before it.
'Did you say impresario?' Arlette keeps the familiar 'you' with Camille, as earlier. The past action uses 'have' followed by 'said'.
'It's classier than agent.' Camille answers with a comparison: 'more' before the description, followed by the small word for 'than'. Arlette then calls her dog.

'Come on, Jean Gabin!' The first word literally means 'go', but here it's just 'come on'. Then a casual command to the dog: 'come'. And now the whole scene again, without stopping. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more.
Je passais par là. Il jouait avec un contrat.
J'en doute. Jean Gabin déteste les contrats.
Il n'a jamais joué avec un contrat.
Moi, c'est Camille. Je pars aujourd'hui.
On dit que vous êtes la plus grande imprésario de Paris.
That was a lovely little meeting: one woman uses the casual 'you', the other the polite one, and you can now hear the difference. See you next time!
